clue.text: A greetings telegram, perhaps, could be a hanging matter !

explanation.surface: A celebratory telegram is imagined as something that could send a person to the gallows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hanging matter' suggests a capital crime, but it means the cord on the back of a framed print. The first sense is a wire (telegram) carrying a picture, as decorated greetings telegrams did.
explanation.definitionFit: A telegram was called a wire, and a greetings one came on a decorated form; the cord strung behind a framed painting holds it on the wall.

clue.text: Suitable wear for a tug-of-war ?

parts.note: reads as sports kit; really a knitted jumper whose name, split, is the command to haul the rope across

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what to wear for a rope-pulling contest.
explanation.walkthrough: A knitted sweater, called a jumper in Britain, has a name that splits into 'pull over', just what a tug-of-war team tries to do to its rivals.
explanation.definitionFit: A knitted top drawn on over the head, which teams try to pull rivals across the line in.

clue.text: No hand at recording the silver collection !

definitions.text: No hand at recording the silver collection

parts.words: No hand at recording the silver collection
parts.note: reads as a poor clerk; really an elegant style of handwriting whose name is also a plate of copper coins, not silver

explanation.surface: Someone is hopeless at keeping track of the church silver.
explanation.walkthrough: The ornate handwriting style is a 'hand'; split, it is a collection plate holding copper coins, the opposite of a silver collection.
explanation.definitionFit: A neat, looped style of writing once engraved on copper plates for printing.

clue.text: Complete agreement with Bob in trade association

indicators.note: the shilling sits in the middle of the word for a trade association

parts.note: a trade union is an association of workers in a trade
a bob was a British shilling, abbreviated s

explanation.surface: Workers in a union with a man named Bob are all of one mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a name, but it is old British slang for a shilling, written s; 'in' puts S inside UNION.
explanation.definitionFit: Voices in unison sound together, so the phrase means total accord.

clue.text: Is Lee involved with her ?

indicators.note: involved means turned and tangled, so the letters of the two words are mixed

explanation.surface: A man named Lee is asked whether he has a romance with a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' looks like a romantic entanglement but rearranges ISLEE into a woman's name, the 'her' of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Elsie is a girl's name, so the woman referred to as she.

clue.text: As a rule a fashionable commander ?

parts.note: something fashionable is in
a general is an army commander

explanation.surface: A stylish military officer is said to be the norm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a rule' looks like an officer's regulations, but 'As a rule' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean usually, for the most part.

clue.text: Time passing in pleasing fashion

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape, so the letters of the word before are reshaped

explanation.surface: The hours are going by agreeably.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fashion' looks like 'manner' in 'in pleasing fashion', but it reshapes PLEASING.
explanation.definitionFit: Time that is elapsing is slipping by.

clue.text: A little drink for the dustman ?

explanation.surface: A refuse collector is offered a small nip of something.
explanation.walkthrough: In old British slang 'totting' was salvaging saleable items from rubbish, and each salvaged item was a tot: something kept back by the dustman (a refuse collector).
explanation.definitionFit: A small measure of spirits is a tot, and so is a scavenged piece of junk in rag-and-bone slang.

clue.text: Company number

explanation.surface: A firm is given a figure.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'two's company, three's a crowd' makes the first definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says a pair makes company; and it is a numeral.

clue.text: Appointment to meet in Coventry Street

indicators.note: in means the letters sit inside the street's name

explanation.surface: A rendezvous is arranged in a London street.
explanation.walkthrough: Hidden in 'CovenTRY STreet'; Coventry Street is a real street near Piccadilly Circus in London.
explanation.definitionFit: A tryst is a meeting arranged in advance, often by lovers.

clue.text: The great artist sounds saucy !

indicators.note: the clue says the artist's name sounds like a word, so a word said aloud is wanted

parts.note: saucy, cheeky in speech, is lippy in British slang

explanation.surface: An Old Master turns out to be cheeky.
explanation.walkthrough: Filippo Lippi was a Florentine painter of the fifteenth century; his surname is said like 'lippy', British slang for impudent.
explanation.definitionFit: Fra Filippo Lippi and his son Filippino were Renaissance painters.

clue.text: A party to an agreement to subscribe to a party

parts.note: to subscribe is literally to write one's name below, to sign
the Tories are a British political party

explanation.surface: Someone joining a pact is asked to put their name down for a political party.
explanation.walkthrough: The two uses of 'party' differ: first one side to a contract (the definition), then a political party, the Tories, Britain's Conservatives.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone who has put a name to a treaty or contract is one of its parties.

clue.text: Laborious, if poetic, call to a flower to unfold

parts.note: ope is a poetic form of open, to unfold; 'if poetic' warns of the archaic word
a rose is a flower

explanation.surface: A poet addresses a bloom, urging it to open its petals.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is the line a poet might write: 'Ope, rose!', a call to the flower to open.
explanation.definitionFit: Operose is a rare literary adjective for something needing great effort, toilsome.

clue.text: Being born in Scotland with no sense of smell ?

indicators.note: the clue asks for the phrase as a Scot would say it, so the sound of Scots speech is wanted

parts.note: Scots 'nae' means no, so 'nae scent' is having no smell

explanation.surface: A baby is delivered in Scotland without any sense of smell.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scots 'nae scent' (no scent) is said much like the English adjective for something coming into being.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nascent is just emerging or coming into existence.

clue.text: He manages to pull the wires in his job

definitions.text: He manages to pull the wires in his job

parts.words: He manages to pull the wires in his job
parts.note: reads as someone pulling strings to get ahead; really a tradesman who literally pulls cable through walls

explanation.surface: A manager pulls strings to keep his position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pull the wires' sounds like 'pull strings', using influence, but here it is the tradesman threading cable.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman who installs and repairs wiring.

clue.text: Show-business in Montreal

parts.note: reads as the entertainment trade of a Canadian city; really the World's Fair of 1967 held there, an exhibition

explanation.surface: The entertainment industry in a Canadian city is under discussion.
explanation.walkthrough: Montreal hosted the 1967 World's Fair, known by a short word for an exhibition; 'show-business' becomes the business of putting on a show.
explanation.definitionFit: A short name for a large trade exhibition or world's fair, like the one held in Montreal in 1967.

clue.text: A little supper dish for one of seven

definitions.text: A little supper dish for one of seven

parts.words: A little supper dish for one of seven
parts.note: reads as a small meal for a diner; really the little porridge bowl each of Snow White's seven dwarfs ate from

explanation.surface: A modest evening meal is served to one member of a group of seven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supper dish' looks like a meal, but it is the bowl itself; the seven are the dwarfs of the fairy tale, each with a little bowl.
explanation.definitionFit: A small bowl with a handle, traditionally for porridge or soup, as each dwarf has in the story.

clue.text: D-Day operation's bosses

explanation.surface: The commanders behind the Normandy landings are named.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1944 Allied invasion of Normandy was Operation Overlord; with the possessive it gives the letters of the second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Operation Overlord was the code name for the D-Day landings; supreme rulers or masters are lords over others.

clue.text: Like Argus. 100 per cent watchful

parts.note: Argus of Greek myth had a hundred eyes, so his watch is a hundred times over: every eye kept awake

explanation.surface: A mythical guardian is completely vigilant.
explanation.walkthrough: '100 per cent' looks like 'totally' but counts Argus's hundred eyes, all kept unclosed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being alert and watchful means keeping one's eyes unclosed.

clue.text: Happen upon a miniature railway in a lane ?

parts.note: to chance upon something is to happen upon it
RY is a short form of railway; 'miniature' signals the shortening

explanation.surface: Someone stumbles across a model railway running down a country lane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'miniature' looks like a toy railway, but it asks for the short form RY. Chancery Lane is a London street of lawyers.
explanation.definitionFit: Chancery Lane is a street in London, so the word is found in a lane's name.

clue.text: Coming men

parts.note: reads as rising stars; really the clan of the Scottish song that announces they are coming

explanation.surface: Promising young men on their way up are described.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scottish song 'The Campbells are Coming' names a Highland clan; 'coming men' sounds like future leaders.
explanation.definitionFit: The Highland clan in the old song are the men who are coming.

clue.text: State of some without a home of their own

indicators.note: 'some of' the following words points to letters taken from within them

explanation.surface: A homeland for a people who have no home of their own.
explanation.walkthrough: The state is concealed in 'withOUT A Home'; the surface also recalls the Mormons, a people seeking a home who settled there.
explanation.definitionFit: Utah is one of the fifty United States.

clue.text: The farmer's news may do so, in conversation

definitions.text: The farmer's news may do so, in conversation

parts.words: The farmer's news may do so, in conversation
parts.note: reads as a topic arising in talk; also the farmer's report that his harvest is up

explanation.surface: A farmer's news comes up while people are chatting.
explanation.walkthrough: A subject that arises in talk does this, and a farmer's news may be that his crop is up.
explanation.definitionFit: To arise unexpectedly, as a topic does in conversation.

clue.text: "—— spirit of the chainless mind!" (Byron)

parts.note: a quotation with a blank: the opening word of Byron's Sonnet on Chillon, describing the spirit of freedom

explanation.surface: A line of Byron praising liberty is quoted with its first word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The solver supplies the missing word of Byron's line, which opens his Sonnet on Chillon, about a prisoner of the castle of Chillon.
explanation.definitionFit: Byron calls the spirit of freedom undying, everlasting, in the first word of his sonnet.

clue.text: One needs room for a bender

definitions.text: One needs room for a bender

parts.words: One needs room for a bender
parts.note: reads as a drinker needing space for a spree; really the arm joint that needs space to bend

explanation.surface: Someone needs space for a drinking spree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bender' is British slang for a drinking bout, but here it is a joint that bends; the phrase 'elbow room' means space.
explanation.definitionFit: The joint of the arm bends, and one speaks of needing room for it.

clue.text: A particular form of vin rosé

definitions.text: A particular form of vin rosé

indicators.note: a form of the words is a reshaping of their letters, so the pink wine's name is rearranged

explanation.surface: One specific style of pink wine is being described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form of' rearranges VINROSE; the result is itself a particular form of those letters, so the whole clue defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A version is one particular variant or rendering of something.

clue.text: Aesop's " biter bit ". according to the file

definitions.text: Aesop's " biter bit ". according to the file

parts.words: Aesop's " biter bit ". according to the file
parts.note: Aesop's fable has a snake that bites a metal file and only hurts itself, the biter bitten

explanation.surface: A dossier describes a case from Aesop of the biter being bitten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the file' looks like a dossier but is the metal rasp of the fable 'The Viper and the File', where the snake tries to bite it.
explanation.definitionFit: In Aesop's fable a venomous snake bites a file and gets hurt itself.

clue.text: The catch on the door ?

parts.note: reads as a latch; really a bucket balanced on a door left ajar to drench whoever opens it

explanation.surface: Someone examines the latch fitted to a door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch' looks like a latch, but it is a trick that catches the unwary, such as the bucket of water above a half-open door.
explanation.definitionFit: A prank or hidden device rigged to spring on whoever disturbs it, like a bucket propped over a door.

clue.text: 7 is, but is not — strange !

explanation.surface: A number is described as both odd and not odd, which is strange.
explanation.walkthrough: The number seven is not even, but the answer at 7 (TWO at 7-down) is even.
explanation.definitionFit: Seven is an uneven number while two is not, and peculiar things are also called this.

clue.text: "To love the game beyond the ——" (Newbolt)

definitions.text: To love the game beyond the

parts.words: To love the game beyond the
parts.note: a quotation with its last word blank, from Newbolt's poem Vitai Lampada about playing for the sake of the sport

explanation.surface: A line from a poem about sportsmanship is quoted with its final word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Newbolt's 'Vitai Lampada' ('Play up! play up! and play the game!') praises loving the game more than the reward for winning it.
explanation.definitionFit: The award for winning, which Newbolt says the true sportsman values less than the game itself.

clue.text: Backward bird of many notes

indicators.note: the bird's name is read backwards, signalled by the word sitting before it

parts.note: a daw, or jackdaw, is a bird

explanation.surface: A bird that sings many notes is reluctant to come forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backward' turns DAW to give a thick roll of banknotes; the surface pretends the notes are birdsong.
explanation.definitionFit: A wad is a thick bundle of paper money.

clue.text: There's some disagreement about altering candy prices

indicators.note: altering the two words changes the order of their letters

explanation.surface: Shoppers argue over changes in what sweets cost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'altering' shuffles CANDY PRICES; 'There's some' and 'about' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: A discrepancy is a lack of agreement between figures or accounts.
